When routine testing is unnecessary

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

A well-appearing 18-month-old has a typical barking cough, hoarseness and mild stridor only when upset after a viral prodrome. There is no drooling, focal chest finding or choking history. Which diagnostic approach is most appropriate?

  1. Clinical diagnosis without routine laboratory testing or imaging
  2. Lateral neck radiography before giving a corticosteroid
  3. Routine viral PCR to select a croup-specific antiviral
  4. Blood culture and inflammatory markers for every episode
  5. Bronchoscopy to exclude a congenital narrowing at the first typical episode
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

Clinical diagnosis without routine laboratory testing or imaging

Typical uncomplicated croup is a clinical diagnosis; unnecessary procedures can distress the child without changing care.

Understanding the options

Clinical diagnosis without routine laboratory testing or imaging
Typical uncomplicated croup is a clinical diagnosis; unnecessary procedures can distress the child without changing care.
Lateral neck radiography before giving a corticosteroid
A typical uncomplicated presentation does not require radiographic confirmation before treatment.
Routine viral PCR to select a croup-specific antiviral
Routine viral identification generally does not guide treatment of typical croup.
Blood culture and inflammatory markers for every episode
These are not routinely indicated in a well-appearing child with a typical presentation.
Bronchoscopy to exclude a congenital narrowing at the first typical episode
Airway endoscopy is reserved for selected atypical or recurrent patterns rather than routine typical croup.
